Oncology is the branch of medicine concerned with the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. Mathematical models can be used to study how cancer develops, grows, and spreads. By providing quantitative and predictive frameworks, mathematical models allow hypotheses about cancer to be tested and evaluated. A carcinogen is any substance that causes cancer. Carcinogenesis is the process by which normal cells are transformed into cancer cells. A key observation that motivated many mathematical models of carcinogenesis is cancer incidence. Cancer incidence often increases rapidly with age, while the occurrence of cancer in an individual appears highly stochastic. However, patterns emerge when cancer incidence is examined across populations. These observations contributed to the development of multistage theories of carcinogenesis, which describe cancer development as a sequence of stages or changes in cells. Beginning in the 1920s, experiments involving chemical carcinogens provided evidence for the idea that cancer develops through multiple stages. In particular, applying two different carcinogens in sequence often produced higher cancer rates than applying a single carcinogen over time, leading to the two-stage model of carcinogenesis. Charles and Luce-Clausen developed one of the first quantitative multistage theories in the 1940s, using a mathematical model to describe the development of skin tumors in mice. Their work demonstrated how mathematical models could be used to connect assumptions about cellular changes with observed cancer incidence. Armitage and Doll further developed multistage theory in the 1950s, introducing more general mathematical models that allowed different rates for different stages and treated the stages as sequential cellular changes rather than necessarily genetic mutations. Their work helped establish mathematical modelling as a framework for studying the development of cancer. 2.3 What is a Mathematical Model? A mathematical model is a numerical representation of a real-world problem. By replacing physical experimentation with mathematical simulations, it allows researchers to evaluate system dynamics and predict future outcomes. 2.4 Systems of ODEs as Mathematical Models A system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) is a set of equations that involves two or more dependent variables that depend on one independent variable. A solution to this system is a set of functions that satisfies each equation on some interval \(I\). A system of ODEs can serve as a mathematical model by describing real world systems where multiple interacting components evolve over a shared independent variable. For example, in ecology, the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model uses a system of two coupled ODEs to track the interdependent population sizes of two interacting species over time \(t\). Many mathematical models are described using systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). It is useful to identify equilibrium points of a system of ODEs and study the stability of the equilibria. Consider the following system of ODEs: \[ rac{dx}{dt} = f(x,y)\] \[ rac{dy}{dt} = g(x,y)\] 2.5 Review of Mathematical Concepts 2.5.1 The Characteristic Equation For a square matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n 	imes n}\), the characteristic equation is given by \(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\). This yields an \(n\)-degree polynomial whose roots correspond directly to the matrix’s eigenvalues \(\lambda\). 2.5.2 The Jacobian Matrix For a vector-valued function \(f: \mathbb{R}^n 	o \mathbb{R}^m\) given by \(f(x) = (f_1(x), \dots, f_m(x))\) where \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\), the Jacobian matrix \(J\) is the \(m 	imes n\) matrix of first-order partial derivatives: \[J =  egin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_n} \ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ \dfrac{\partial f_m}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial f_m}{\partial x_n} \end{pmatrix}\] When \(m=n\), i.e., the matrix is square, its determinant, commonly referred to as the Jacobian, acts as a local scaling factor. The Jacobian plays an essential role in coordinate transformations by describing how areas or volumes stretch, rotate, and distort under a change of variables. Consider the system of ODEs above. The Jacobian matrix of the system is \[J(x,y)=  egin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\ \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix}\] This matrix contains the first order partial derivatives of \(f\) and \(g\), describing how small changes in \(x\) and \(y\) affect the rate of change of the system. 2.5.3 Equilibrium Points and Local Stability An equilibrium point is a point \((x^*, y^*)\) such that \( rac{dx}{dt} = 0\) and \( rac{dy}{dt} = 0\). That is, an equilibrium point is a point at which both variables \(x\) and \(y\) remain constant over time. At an equilibrium, there is no net change in either variable. It is important to note that the equilibrium of a system does not mean that individual processes affecting \(x\) and \(y\) have stopped. Rather, the processes are balancing each other. Finding an equilibrium tells us where a system can remain unchanged, but does not tell us what happens if the system is slightly disturbed. Stability describes how a system behaves following a small deviation from an equilibrium. An equilibrium is stable if solutions that start sufficiently close to the equilibrium remain close to it. An equilibrium is asymptotically stable, if it is stable and solutions that start sufficiently close will eventually approach the equilibrium. An equilibrium is unstable if it is not stable. To study the local stability of an equilibrium \((x^*, y^*)\), we analyse the eigenvalues of \(J(x^*, y^*)\). Let \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) be eigenvalues of \(J(x^*, y^*)\), and \((x^*, y^*)\) an equilibrium point. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both real and negative, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is asymptotically stable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both real and positive, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is unstable. If \(\lambda _ 1 < 0\) and \(\lambda_2 > 0\), with both being real, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is called a saddle point and is unstable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both complex with negative real parts, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is asymptotically stable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both complex with positive real parts, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is unstable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both purely imaginary, then the linearized system exhibits oscillatory behaviour. Further analysis is required to determine stability. Chapter 3 The Kuznetsov Tumour–Immune Model A tumour is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and divide more than they should or do not die when they should. Tumours may be benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer). Malignant tumours can spread into, or invade, nearby tissues. They can also spread to other parts of the body through the blood and lymph systems. Tumour cells reproduce and therefore could increase the tumour population. Moreover, tumour cells can also be removed through interactions with immune effector cells. These cells recognize and respond to abnormal cells, including tumour cells. Some examples of these cells are cytotoxic T lymphocytes and natural killer cells. Define the following: \(E\): Number of effector cells located at the tumor site, \(T\): Number of tumor cells located at the tumor site, \(s\): Baseline rate at which mature effector cells enter the tumour region, \(p\): Rate of tumour stimulated effector cell accumulation \(g\): Saturation parameter for tumour stimulated effector cell accumulation, \(m\): Rate of effector cell inactivation due to interactions with tumour cells, \(n\): Rate of tumour cell killing through interactions with effector cells, \(d\): Rate of ordinary effector cell elimination \(a\): Maximum growth rate of the tumor cell population, \(b\): Inverse of maximum carrying capacity, where all of the above parameters are constant. To determine the rate of change of the effector cell population, we consider processes that increase and decrease the number of effector cells. Effector cells enter the tumour region at baseline rate \(s\). Tumour cells also stimulate the accumulation of effector cells. We assume that this stimulation increases with tumour cell number but eventually saturates, giving the term \( rac{pET}{g+T}\). The saturation reflects the assumption that the accumulation of effector cells cannot increase indefinitely as tumour size increases, due to biological limitations. Effector cells are also inactivated through interactions with tumour cells at a rate proportional to both \(E\) and \(T\), giving the term \(mET\). Finally, effector cells are eliminated naturally at a rate proportional to the size of the population, giving the term \(dE\). Combining these processes together, we obtain: \[ egin{equation}  rac{dE}{dt} = s +  rac{pET}{g+T} - mET -dE \label{eq:kuznetsov4a} \end{equation}\] Similarly, to determine the rate of change of the tumour cell population, we consider processes that increase and decrease the number of tumour cells. We assume that tumour cells undergo logistic growth. At low tumour cell numbers, growth is approximately exponential, while at high tumour cell numbers, growth slows due to limitations such as available resources. This gives the logistic growth term \(aT(1-bT)\). Tumour cells are also removed through interactions with immune effector cells. We assume that the rate of tumour cell killing is proportional to both the number of tumour cells and the number of effector cells, giving the term \(nET\). Chapter 4 Extending the Model: An Immune-Resistant Tumor Subpopulation 4.1 Motivation and model equations The Kuznetsov model of Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\) treats the tumor as a single, immunologically uniform population. Real tumors, however, are heterogeneous, and subclones that partially evade immune-mediated killing are a central driver of treatment failure. As a first extension, we equip the tumor cell population \(T\) with a degree of immune resistance, benchmarked directly against the Kuznetsov model so that setting the resistance parameters to their “no resistance” values recovers Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\) exactly. The model presented here is the single-subpopulation special case of a more general two-subpopulation (immune-resistant vs. immune-sensitive, with optional chemotherapy resistance) model developed in , to which we refer the reader for the full treatment, including both immune-evasion mechanisms considered simultaneously with chemotherapy. We assume resistance carries a growth-rate cost \(\zeta>0\), so the resistant population’s growth rate is \(\alpha_T=\alpha-\zeta\) rather than the wild-type rate \(\alpha\), and confers a benefit \(\theta\in[0,1]\) that reduces the effectiveness of effector-mediated killing (\(\theta=1\) recovers full susceptibility, i.e. no resistance). Writing \(E\) for the effector population and \(\kappa=1/\beta\) for the carrying capacity, the dynamics are This is structurally identical to \(\eqref{eq:kuz_ODEs}\): tumor growth is logistic and suppressed by effector-mediated killing at rate \(\theta E\); effectors are produced at baseline rate \(\sigma\), activated through a saturating term with parameters \(\rho_T,\eta\), exhausted or inactivated by the tumor at rate \(\mu_T\), and die naturally at rate \(\delta\). The only change is that the activation and inactivation parameters, \(\rho_T\) and \(\mu_T\), and the effective growth rate \(\alpha_T\) and kill-rate reduction \(\theta\), now depend on the resistance mechanism the tumor employs, as derived mechanistically below. Setting \(\theta=1\), \(\alpha_T=\alpha\), \(\rho_T=\rho\), \(\mu_T=\mu\) recovers \(\eqref{eq:kuz_ODEs}\) exactly, confirming this is a proper extension rather than a different model. 4.2 Mechanistic derivation of \(\theta\), \(\rho_T\), and \(\mu_T\) As in the Kuznetsov model, effectors and tumor cells transiently bind to form a conjugate \(C\), which then dissociates leaving either cell undamaged, the tumor cell lethally hit, or the effector cell inactivated (Figure \(\ref{fig:red_ET_diagram}\)). Immune resistance is modeled as a change in the rates governing this reaction scheme relative to a wild-type (non-resistant) baseline, denoted with a superscript \((0)\). Assuming the conjugate dynamics equilibrate on a fast time scale relative to cell division and death (the same quasi-steady-state argument used in to derive \(\eqref{eq:kuz_ODEs}\) from the underlying reaction scheme), we have \(C = \Gamma E T\) with \(\Gamma = \gamma_1/(\gamma_{-1}+\gamma_2+\gamma_3)\). After rescaling by the wild-type reference rate \(\gamma_2^{(0)}\Gamma^{(0)}\), the reduced system \(\eqref{eq:red_ODEs}\) follows with \[\begin{equation} \theta = \frac{\gamma_2\Gamma}{\gamma_2^{(0)}\Gamma^{(0)}}, \qquad \rho_T=\rho\,\frac{\Gamma}{\Gamma^{(0)}}, \qquad \mu_T = \frac{\gamma_3\Gamma}{\gamma_2^{(0)}\Gamma^{(0)}}. \end{equation}\] We consider two concrete resistance mechanisms: The distinction between the two mechanisms is therefore whether resistance acts on the of an effector–tumor encounter (checkpoint evasion) or on the of encounter itself (reduced antigen presentation). Table \(\ref{tbl:red_param}\) summarizes the parameters of the extended model, reusing the Kuznetsov baseline values from Table \(\ref{tbl:kuz_param}\) for all quantities unrelated to resistance. 4.3 Equilibria and stability The system \(\eqref{eq:red_ODEs}\) admits a tumor-free equilibrium \(\mathcal{E}_0 = (0, \sigma/\delta)\) – identical in form to the Kuznetsov tumor-free state, since resistance only affects the dynamics once \(T>0\) – and, when it exists, a tumor-present equilibrium \(\mathcal{E}_1=(T^*,E^*)\) with \(T^*>0\). Exactly as in Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\), the Jacobian at \(\mathcal{E}_0\) is triangular, with eigenvalues \[\begin{equation} \lambda_1 = \alpha_T - \theta\,\frac{\sigma}{\delta}, \qquad \lambda_2 = -\delta, \end{equation}\] giving the following direct generalization of Proposition \(\ref{prop_kuz_tumorfree}\). At a tumor-present equilibrium, \(T^*\) and \(E^*\) satisfy \[\begin{equation} E^* = \alpha_T\left(1-\frac{T^*}{\kappa}\right) = \frac{\sigma}{\dfrac{\rho_T T^*}{T^*+\eta} - \mu_T T^* - \delta}. \label{eq:red_eq_condition} \end{equation}\] 4.4 Root structure and sign test Clearing denominators in Equation \(\eqref{eq:red_eq_condition}\), exactly as was done for the Kuznetsov model in Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\), gives the cubic polynomial \[\begin{equation} F(T^*) = B_3 T^{*3} + B_2 T^{*2} + B_1 T^* + B_0 = 0, \label{eq:red_cubic} \end{equation}\] with coefficients One can check directly that \(B_i = \alpha_T\kappa\,C_i'\) for \(i=0,\dots,3\), where \(C_i'\) denotes the Kuznetsov coefficient \(C_i\) of Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\) with \((\alpha,\rho,\mu,\beta)\) replaced by \((\alpha_T,\rho_T,\mu_T,1/\kappa)\). Since multiplying a polynomial by the positive constant \(\alpha_T\kappa\) does not change its roots, \(\eqref{eq:red_cubic}\) has exactly the same positive-root structure as the Kuznetsov cubic with resistant parameters substituted in – confirming that resistance enters the equilibrium problem only by remapping the same three parameters that already governed the wild-type dynamics. The same four-step sign test from Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\) therefore applies verbatim: As before, the sign sequence \((+,-,+,-)\) has three sign changes, so Descartes’ Rule predicts either one or three positive roots of \(\eqref{eq:red_cubic}\), with three being the generic case – the hallmark of bistability between a low- and a high-tumor-burden resistant equilibrium. This is exactly the qualitative structure established for the Kuznetsov model in Section \(\ref{sec:kuznetsov}\), now shown to persist under both forms of immune resistance considered here, provided effector activation continues to dominate tumor-induced exhaustion (\(\rho_T>\mu_T\eta+\delta\)) at the resistant phenotype’s parameter values. The Jacobian at \(\mathcal{E}_1\) is \[\begin{equation} J(\mathcal{E}_1) = \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{\alpha_T}{\kappa}T^* & -\theta T^* \\[8pt] E^*\left(\dfrac{\rho_T\eta}{(T^*+\eta)^2} - \mu_T\right) & -\dfrac{\sigma}{E^*} \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation}\] with \(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(J(\mathcal{E}_1))<0\) and \[\begin{equation} \det(J(\mathcal{E}_1)) = \frac{\alpha_T\sigma}{\kappa E^*}T^* + \left(\frac{\rho_T\eta}{(T^*+\eta)^2}-\mu_T\right)\theta E^* T^*. \end{equation}\] As in the wild-type model, \(\mathcal{E}_1\) is stable whenever \(\det(J(\mathcal{E}_1))>0\), which holds in particular if \(\rho_T\eta/(T^*+\eta)^2 > \mu_T\); otherwise, bistability between a low- and high-tumor-burden resistant equilibrium arises via the usual saddle-node bifurcation structure, consistent with the three-root sign-test result above.

Chapter 5 Summary Starting from the two-population Kuznetsov tumor–immune model, we showed that its coexistence-equilibrium structure is governed by a cubic polynomial whose coefficient signs – not its explicit roots – determine whether the system is monostable or bistable. The same sign-test machinery, applied unchanged after remapping three parameters to account for a resistant phenotype, shows that an immune-resistant tumor subpopulation inherits the same qualitative bistability whenever effector activation continues to dominate tumor-induced exhaustion at the resistant phenotype’s parameter values. This worked example illustrates a general strategy for analyzing tumor–immune models in this course: reduce the equilibrium condition to a low-degree polynomial, and use a sign test on its coefficients, rather than brute-force root-finding, to characterize the number and type of biologically admissible steady states. % %

In reality, however, cancer is driven by three factors: individual differences between cells, competition for space, and direct interactions with their surroundings. To capture these biological dynamics in a computer simulation, Agent-Based Models (ABMs) rely on four core building blocks: 6.3.1 Agents and State Variables Agents are independent computational entities representing individual biological actors (for example, tumor cells, cytotoxic T lymphocytes, macrophages, or stromal fibroblasts). Each agent maintains its own internal state variables, which may include: Spatial Coordinates: Position \((x, y)\) on a discrete lattice or continuous coordinate space. Agent Type / Phenotype: Cell lineage (e.g., prey/tumor cell vs. predator/immune cell, stem-like vs. differentiated, sensitive vs. drug-resistant). Internal Resources / Health: Energy level, cell volume, or damage accumulation (e.g., DNA double-strand breaks). Lifecycle Status: Active/proliferating, quiescent, senescent, or flagged for death (apoptotic/necrotic). 6.3.2 Environment (The World) The environment represents the physical tissue domain and biochemical landscape in which agents live: Spatial Topology: Typically presented as a 2D or 3D grid. The boundaries can be reflective (rigid walls) or periodic (wrapping around edges so cells exiting the right re-enter on the left). Physical Exclusion: Rules dictating whether a single lattice site can host multiple agents or enforces volume control (carrying capacity per cell). Background resources: Gradients of extracellular nutrients (glucose, oxygen), chemokines, or therapeutic drugs that diffuse, decay, and are consumed by agents. 6.3.3 Interaction and Behavior Rules Rules define how each cell behaves and makes decisions at every step of the simulation. Some examples include: Movement: Random walks, contact-inhibited crawling, or chemotaxis toward nutrient sources. Feeding & Metabolism: Extracting energy from the local environment or prey to fuel baseline basal metabolic costs. Immune Attacks (Predation): Immune cells spotting cancer cells upon physical proximity, causing them to lock onto them and destroy them (cell lysis). Reproduction (Proliferation): Dividing into daughter cells when internal energy exceeds a threshold and space is available. Cell Death (Apoptosis): Cell death triggered by starvation (energy dropping below zero), immune destruction, or senescence. 6.3.4 Iterative Scheduling Loop Time advances in discrete increments (\(\Delta t\)). At each time step: Activation Order: Living agents are activated. In asynchronous scheduling, the order is randomized at every step to prevent execution order artifacts. Action Execution: Each agent evaluates its local neighborhood, updates its energy, moves, interacts, and potentially reproduces or dies. Environmental Update: Diffusive fields diffuse/decay and renewable resources regenerate. State Census: Macroscopic summary statistics (e.g., total population counts, spatial clustering) are logged for analysis. 6.4 Hands-On Implementation Walkthrough: Tumour-Immune Dynamics in R & Plotly In Chapter 1, we introduced the classic Lotka-Volterra system to describe predator-prey interactions between cytotoxic immune effector cells (\(E\), predators) and tumour cells (\(T\), prey): \[\frac{dT}{dt} = a\, T - b\, T E, \qquad \frac{dE}{dt} = c\, T E - d\, E\] In continuous ordinary differential equations (ODEs), populations are assumed to be “well-mixed” and uniformly distributed across continuous space. However, real clinical tumors grow in complex, structured physical microenvironments where space and local biology govern survival: Spatial Clustering & Nodule Formation: Tumours do not disperse evenly; they originate as dense, localized nodules surrounded by healthy tissue and vascular beds. Contact Inhibition (Volume Exclusion): Cells require physical room to divide. Even if nutrients are abundant, cells tightly packed in the tumor core cannot proliferate until space opens up at the tumor margin. Chemotaxis (Directed Search): Immune cells do not wander blindly. Instead, they sense chemical gradients (chemokines) secreted by tumour cells, migrating preferentially toward cancer nests. T-Cell Exhaustion: Chronic antigenic stimulation causes cytotoxic T cells to become functionally exhausted, losing their ability to kill or proliferate. Therapeutic Rescue (Immunotherapy): Immune checkpoint inhibitors (such as anti-PD-1 / anti-PD-L1 antibodies) block inhibitory pathways, reinvigorating exhausted T cells and restoring immune control. Here, we translate these Lotka-Volterra tumour-immune dynamics into an Agent-Based Model (ABM). They take up nutrients supplied by nearby blood vessels to fuel their basic survival, move into open surrounding areas, and multiply until they run out of room (contact-inhibited growth). T-cell recruitment rate per 100 tumour cells chemotaxis = 0.60, # Chemotactic bias toward neighbouring tumour therapy = FALSE, # Checkpoint inhibitor therapy active? therapy_start = 200, # Step at which therapy is initiated therapy_kill_boost = 1.6, # Multiplier for kill probability under therapy therapy_exh_mult = 4, # Multiplier for exhaustion limit under therapy seed = 1 # Random seed for reproducible results ) 6.4.3.2 Step 2: Initializing the Model Environment The initialize_model() function builds the tissue lattice, seeds the central tumor nodule, places patrolling T cells, and sets up the vascular nutrient grid. initialize_model <- function(p = default_params) { set.seed(p$seed) # Fix seed for reproducible scientific simulations m <- new.env() # Create our mutable simulation environment W <- H <- as.integer(p$dims) m$W <- W m$H <- H m$p <- p # --- Seed the Central Tumour Nodule --- # In vivo tumors originate as compact masses. # To mimic this, we calculate each lattice site's distance from the center, add a small amount of random noise, # and pick the nearest sites to form a naturally rounded cluster. cx <- (W + 1) / 2 cy <- (H + 1) / 2 all_sites <- expand.grid(x = seq_len(W), y = seq_len(H)) distances <- sqrt((all_sites$x - cx)^2 + (all_sites$y - cy)^2) ordered_sites <- all_sites[order(distances + runif(nrow(all_sites), 0, 0.5)), ] nt <- min(p$n_tumour, W * H) tx <- ordered_sites$x[seq_len(nt)] ty <- ordered_sites$y[seq_len(nt)] # --- Seed Patrolling T Cells --- # T cells begin scattered randomly across the tissue microenvironment ncel <- p$n_tcell n_total <- nt + ncel # --- Populate Parallel Attribute Vectors --- m$type <- c(rep(TUMOUR, nt), rep(TCELL, ncel)) m$x <- c(tx, sample.int(W, ncel, replace = TRUE)) m$y <- c(ty, sample.int(H, ncel, replace = TRUE)) m$energy <- as.numeric(c( sample.int(2 * p$de_tumour, nt, replace = TRUE) - 1, sample.int(2 * p$de_tcell, ncel, replace = TRUE) - 1 )) m$kills <- integer(n_total) # Cumulative kills per agent (tracks exhaustion) m$alive <- rep(TRUE, n_total) # Life status: TRUE = active, FALSE = removed # --- Spatial Matrix (Volume Exclusion) --- # Holds the agent ID of the occupying tumour cell, or 0 if vacant m$tum <- matrix(0L, W, H) m$tum[cbind(tx, ty)] <- seq_len(nt) # --- Vascular Nutrient Field --- # TRUE = nutrient patch available; countdown = remaining steps until replenishment m$fully <- matrix(sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), W * H, replace = TRUE), W, H) m$countdown <- matrix( ifelse(m$fully, p$resupply_time, sample.int(p$resupply_time, W * H, replace = TRUE) - 1L), W, H ) # History tracking vectors for population time series m$step <- 0L m$kill_events <- 0L m$h_step <- integer(0) m$h_tumour <- integer(0) m$h_active <- integer(0) m$h_exhausted <- integer(0) m$h_nutrient <- integer(0) record(m) # Take initial census m } 6.4.3.3 Step 3: Helper Functions (Adding, Removing, and Finding Neighbors) These concise helper functions manage agent lifecycle changes, boundary math, and therapy state. # Check whether checkpoint inhibitor therapy is active at the current step therapy_on <- function(m) { m$p$therapy && m$step >= m$p$therapy_start } # Dynamic exhaustion threshold (expanded when immunotherapy is active) exh_limit <- function(m) { m$p$exhaustion_limit * (if (therapy_on(m)) m$p$therapy_exh_mult else 1) } # Dynamic kill probability (boosted when immunotherapy is active) kill_prob <- function(m) { min(1.0, m$p$p_kill * (if (therapy_on(m)) m$p$therapy_kill_boost else 1)) } # Add a newborn daughter cell or newly recruited T cell to our parallel vectors add_agent <- function(m, type, x, y, energy, kills = 0L) { m$type <- c(m$type, type) m$x <- c(m$x, x) m$y <- c(m$y, y) m$energy <- c(m$energy, energy) m$kills <- c(m$kills, kills) m$alive <- c(m$alive, TRUE) new_id <- length(m$alive) if (type == TUMOUR) m$tum[x, y] <- new_id new_id } # Mark a cell as dead and clear its coordinate in the spatial matrix remove_agent <- function(m, i) { m$alive[i] <- FALSE if (m$type[i] == TUMOUR) m$tum[m$x[i], m$y[i]] <- 0L } # Calculate the coordinates of all 8 neighbors with toroidal boundary wrap-around neighbours <- function(m, i) { list( x = ((m$x[i] - 1L + DX) %% m$W) + 1L, y = ((m$y[i] - 1L + DY) %% m$H) + 1L ) } 6.4.3.4 Step 4: Tumour Cell Behavior Rules At each time step, every living tumour cell follows four biological rules: Motility: With probability tumour_motility, it migrates into an unoccupied adjacent patch. Basal Metabolism: It consumes \(1\) unit of energy. If its energy drops below zero, it undergoes necrotic cell death from starvation. Nutrient Uptake: If glucose/oxygen is present at its patch, it takes up the nutrient and gains energy (de_tumour). Contact-Inhibited Proliferation: With probability tumour_div, it divides into an empty adjacent patch, splitting its energy with the daughter cell. If all \(8\) neighboring sites are occupied by other cancer cells, division is physically blocked (contact inhibition). tumour_step <- function(m, i) { p <- m$p nb <- neighbours(m, i) # Identify which of the 8 neighbouring lattice sites are unoccupied free <- m$tum[cbind(nb$x, nb$y)] == 0L # 1. Migration: crawl to an empty neighboring patch if (any(free) && runif(1) < p$tumour_motility) { k <- which(free) k <- k[sample.int(length(k), 1)] # Choose one empty neighbor at random m$tum[m$x[i], m$y[i]] <- 0L # Clear old position m$x[i] <- nb$x[k]; m$y[i] <- nb$y[k] # Update coordinates m$tum[m$x[i], m$y[i]] <- i # Register new position # Re-evaluate empty neighbors after moving nb <- neighbours(m, i) free <- m$tum[cbind(nb$x, nb$y)] == 0L } # 2. Basal Metabolism: expend 1 energy unit for survival m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] - 1 if (m$energy[i] < 0) { remove_agent(m, i) # Starvation: cell undergoes necrosis return(invisible()) } # 3. Nutrient Uptake: feed on vascular glucose/oxygen if (m$fully[m$x[i], m$y[i]]) { m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] + p$de_tumour m$fully[m$x[i], m$y[i]] <- FALSE # Nutrient patch is now depleted } # 4. Proliferation: divide into a free neighboring site (contact-inhibited) if (any(free) && runif(1) <= p$tumour_div) { k <- which(free) k <- k[sample.int(length(k), 1)] m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] / 2 # Parent divides energy equally with daughter cell add_agent(m, TUMOUR, nb$x[k], nb$y[k], m$energy[i]) } } 6.4.3.5 Step 5: Cytotoxic T Cell Behavior Rules Each living T cell acts as a patrolling predator: Chemotaxis & Movement: The T cell evaluates its \(8\) neighboring patches. If any neighbor holds a tumour cell, it steps toward it with probability chemotaxis (chemokine gradient guidance); otherwise, it performs a random walk step. Metabolism & Finite Lifespan: The T cell loses \(1\) energy unit per step. If energy drops below zero, it dies of senescence. Exhaustion Check: If the T cell’s cumulative kill count reaches exhaustion_limit, it becomes exhausted: it remains physically present in the tissue but can no longer attack or proliferate. Contact Cytotoxicity: If active (non-exhausted) and sharing a patch with a tumour cell, it attacks with probability kill_prob, destroying the tumour cell (cell lysis), gaining energy (de_tcell), and logging a kill. Clonal Expansion: Following a kill, with probability tcell_prolif, the T cell divides into two active daughter T cells. tcell_step <- function(m, i) { p <- m$p nb <- neighbours(m, i) # 1. Chemotaxis: sense nearby tumour cells and step toward them nearby_tumours <- which(m$tum[cbind(nb$x, nb$y)] > 0L) k <- if (length(nearby_tumours) > 0 && runif(1) < p$chemotaxis) { nearby_tumours[sample.int(length(nearby_tumours), 1)] # Directed step toward tumor } else { sample.int(8L, 1) # Random exploration step } m$x[i] <- nb$x[k] m$y[i] <- nb$y[k] # 2. Metabolism & Natural Lifespan m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] - 1 if (m$energy[i] < 0) { remove_agent(m, i) # T cell dies of natural senescence return(invisible()) } # 3. Exhaustion Check: exhausted T cells cannot kill or proliferate if (m$kills[i] >= exh_limit(m)) { return(invisible()) } # 4. Contact Cytotoxicity: attack tumour cell at current site target <- m$tum[m$x[i], m$y[i]] if (target > 0L && runif(1) <= kill_prob(m)) { remove_agent(m, target) # Lyse the tumour cell m$kill_events <- m$kill_events + 1L m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] + p$de_tcell m$kills[i] <- m$kills[i] + 1L # 5. Clonal Proliferation: divide following antigenic stimulation if (runif(1) <= p$tcell_prolif) { m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] / 2 # Parent splits energy with daughter T cell add_agent(m, TCELL, m$x[i], m$y[i], m$energy[i], m$kills[i]) } } } 6.4.3.6 Step 6: Environmental Regeneration and Systemic Recruitment Between cellular actions, vascular nutrients replenish and new immune cells enter the tissue from systemic circulation in proportion to tumour antigen load: # Nutrient Regrowth: Depleted vascular patches count down and replenish nutrient_step <- function(m) { R <- m$p$resupply_time growing <- !m$fully ready <- growing & m$countdown <= 0 m$fully[ready] <- TRUE m$countdown[ready] <- R dec <- growing & !ready m$countdown[dec] <- m$countdown[dec] - 1L } # Systemic T-Cell Recruitment: # Bloodborne T cells extravasate into tissue at a rate proportional to tumour antigen load. # The number of new cells arriving each step is sampled from a Poisson distribution. recruit_tcells <- function(m) { n_tum <- sum(m$alive & m$type == TUMOUR) n_new <- rpois(1, m$p$recruit * n_tum / 100) for (j in seq_len(n_new)) { add_agent( m, TCELL, sample.int(m$W, 1), sample.int(m$H, 1), sample.int(2 * m$p$de_tcell, 1) - 1 ) } } # Census function: tallies active, exhausted, and tumour populations counts <- function(m) { a <- m$alive tc <- a & m$type == TCELL exh <- tc & (m$kills >= exh_limit(m)) c( tumour = sum(a & m$type == TUMOUR), active = sum(tc & !exh), exhausted = sum(exh), nutrient = sum(m$fully) ) } # History logger for time-series trajectories record <- function(m) { cc <- counts(m) m$h_step <- c(m$h_step, m$step) m$h_tumour <- c(m$h_tumour, cc[["tumour"]]) m$h_active <- c(m$h_active, cc[["active"]]) m$h_exhausted <- c(m$h_exhausted, cc[["exhausted"]]) m$h_nutrient <- c(m$h_nutrient, cc[["nutrient"]]) } 6.4.3.7 Step 7: The Master Scheduling Loop At each discrete simulation step (\(\Delta t\)), living agents are activated. Notice that we randomly shuffle the execution order (sample.int(...)) so that no individual cell receives an unfair “first-move” advantage at every turn: model_step <- function(m) { # Asynchronous random scheduling: shuffle living agent indices ids <- which(m$alive) ids <- ids[sample.int(length(ids))] for (i in ids) { if (!m$alive[i]) next if (m$type[i] == TUMOUR) tumour_step(m, i) else tcell_step(m, i) } nutrient_step(m) # Regenerate depleted vascular nutrients recruit_tcells(m) # Recruit circulating T cells based on tumour antigen load m$step <- m$step + 1L record(m) # Record population census # Housekeeping: periodically prune dead agents from memory so vectors stay compact if (length(m$alive) > 4 * sum(m$alive) + 500) { keep <- m$alive old_ids <- which(keep) for (v in c("type", "x", "y", "energy", "kills", "alive")) m[[v]] <- m[[v]][keep] remap <- integer(length(keep)) remap[old_ids] <- seq_along(old_ids) m$tum[m$tum > 0L] <- remap[m$tum[m$tum > 0L]] } } 6.4.4 Interactive Visualizations with Plotly 6.4.4.1 1. categorized by the Three “E”s of Cancer Immunoediting: Elimination: The nascent tumor is successfully recognized and eradicated by cytotoxic immune responses. Equilibrium: Tumour cells and immune cells reach a dynamic standoff, keeping the tumor burden stable over extended time scales (the spatial analog of stable Lotka-Volterra coexistence). Escape: Persistent stimulation triggers immune exhaustion and suppresses cytotoxicity, enabling the tumor to break through immune control. 6.4.5.1 Scenario 1: Stable Immune Equilibrium Under our default parameters, the tumor nodule expands until systemic recruitment and chemotaxis mobilize cytotoxic T cells to the tumor boundary, producing a stable standoff: # Initialize the model with default equilibrium parameters sim_equilibrium <- initialize_model(default_params) # Render the interactive in-browser animated player over 25 steps plot_animated_simulation(sim_equilibrium, n_steps = 25) Now let us run the model forward for an additional \(75\) steps (totaling \(100\) steps) and examine the macroscopic population trajectories: # Advance simulation to step 100 for (step in 26:100) { model_step(sim_equilibrium) } # Render final 2D spatial microenvironment snapshot plot_grid(sim_equilibrium) # Render interactive macroscopic population trajectories plot_timeseries(sim_equilibrium) 6.4.5.2 Scenario 2: Immune Escape and Checkpoint Inhibitor Rescue What happens if T-cell exhaustion occurs very rapidly (exhaustion_limit = 2)? The tumor quickly exhausts its attackers and breaks free (immune escape). However, administering checkpoint inhibitor therapy (anti-PD-1) at step \(120\) quadruples the exhaustion limit and boosts killing efficiency, rejuvenating exhausted cells and controlling the escaping tumor. # Configure scenario: low exhaustion limit, with therapy starting at step 120 escape_params <- default_params escape_params$exhaustion_limit <- 2 # Rapid exhaustion triggers immune escape escape_params$therapy <- TRUE # Administer checkpoint inhibitor escape_params$therapy_start <- 120 # Therapy initiated at step 120 escape_params$therapy_kill_boost <- 1.6 # 60% boost to cytotoxicity escape_params$therapy_exh_mult <- 4 # Quadruple exhaustion limit sim_therapy <- initialize_model(escape_params) # Simulate 220 time steps across the pre-treatment and post-treatment phases for (step in 1:220) { model_step(sim_therapy) } # Render interactive time series showing tumor escape and therapeutic rescue plot_timeseries(sim_therapy) Notice how the purple tumour curve initially skyrockets between steps \(40\) and \(120\) as active T cells plummet into exhaustion (the dashed grey curve). The moment checkpoint inhibitor therapy is administered at step \(120\) (indicated by the vertical green marker), exhausted T cells are rapidly reinvigorated, driving tumour eradication! 6.5 Standardized Model Documentation: The ODD Protocol 6.5.1 Motivation: Reproducibility in Computational Modeling (To be developed by Maria) 6.5.2 The Seven Elements of ODD Applied to Cancer Models (To be developed by Maria)
